rules.rule: sections start at a bracket, whatever is open
rules.evil: ]] asks Emacs where this defun ends, by scanning brackets from its start, then steps back from the end of the next one. With a bracket in the first column inside an open one, or one that never closes, it lands inside a line or even moves backward.
rules.die_vim: ]] and [[ go by the lines that start with an opening bracket, outside a string, and nothing else. While brackets balance, and none in the first column is nested in another, that's your Evil's result.

rules.rule: the last line is the last line
rules.evil: The cursor can rest on the empty line after a file's final newline: G, 5j, w, }, dd, dk, dj, dG, L and gj go there, and so does M in a short buffer. j from the last line goes there without an error; j, gj and C-d on the empty line itself fail.
rules.die_vim: What your Evil does when the text has no final newline, with the newline kept: motions never put the cursor on the empty line after it. Motions stop on the last line. j, gj, + and C-d on the last line fail, and so do w and e on its last character and } at its end; a macro ends at the first failure. j doesn't fail when its goal column is past the line's end, as after $: your Evil's j tries that column first, and that moves the cursor. dj, cj and yj on the last line act on that line, as Evil's do (Vim's fail). After dd, dk or dG removes the last lines, the cursor goes to the new last line, in the column the delete started in (S5 row 2). G recentres on the last line, and H, M and L clamp to it. An insert session or an undo can still leave the cursor on that empty line, as in Evil and Vim. Motions along it (0, ^, $, C-a) stay on it, and } from it fails. That empty line still takes a screen row, as in Emacs, so window positions are Evil's. Each fixture takes its cursor and errors from your Evil on the same text without its final newline, and its text and registers from the run with the newline: the run without it adds a - register and has text bugs of its own. A macro that stops a repetition sooner than Evil's takes its registers from the run without the newline, because it deletes less. J on the last line has nothing to join, and the final newline stays; your Evil's J takes it. A count past the last line can't reach the empty line after it, so 2D on the last line takes the line's text, not the whole line.

rules.rule: a count before / or ? finds the nth match
rules.evil: 2/x and 2?x ignore the count.
rules.die_vim: As in Vim: 2/x goes to the second match after the cursor, wrapping past the end as one search does. A later n moves one match.

rules.rule: an empty search repeats the last one
rules.evil: /<CR> does nothing.
rules.die_vim: As in Vim: / or ? with an empty pattern searches for the last pattern again, in its own direction. With no last pattern it's an error.

rules.rule: . inside a macro repeats the macro's change
rules.evil: . inside a macro repeats the last change made before the macro ran, since Evil runs macros without command hooks, so it errors when there is none. After @a, . replays the macro, but errors 'No previous macro' when the macro used an operator such as dw.
rules.die_vim: As in Vim inside a macro: a change made there becomes the last change, so a later . in the same macro repeats it (before any change, . repeats the change made before the macro). After the macro, . replays the macro, as Evil's does, without Evil's 'No previous macro' error when the macro used an operator.

cases.note: . replays the dw and takes the next word; Evil's fails, and macros/dot-replays-macro and macros/dot-after-motion-macro pin the replay

rules.rule: a linewise put over the last line keeps the final newline
rules.evil: Vp (and VP, and Vjp over the last two lines) on the buffer's last line leaves an empty line and drops the final newline.
rules.die_vim: As in Vim: the lines are replaced and the final newline stays.

rules.rule: a count before H counts from 1
rules.evil: nH goes to line n+1 of the window: 3H goes to the fourth line.
rules.die_vim: As in Vim: nH goes to line n of the window, so 3H goes to the third. H, M and L otherwise follow Evil (S5 row 20).

rules.rule: undo is Vim's u and C-r
rules.evil: Your Evil has no redo (evil-undo-system is unset): C-r signals an error, and u after another command redoes, as Emacs's undo chain does.
rules.die_vim: Your S5 answer: u steps back and C-r steps forward, as in Vim (scope §10). C-r with nothing to redo fails, as u with nothing to undo does. Each command is its own step, so a run of ~, J, r or g~ isn't one step, as it is in Emacs. u puts the cursor back where the step's first change was made from, so a J from an empty line stays there, where Evil's u leaves the cursor on the next line.

rules.rule: regular expressions are Rust's
rules.evil: :s/\(foo\) \(bar\)/\2 \1/ uses Emacs regex groups.
rules.die_vim: DIE's regex syntax is Rust's (D4): the same change is :s/(foo) (bar)/$2 $1/, with the same result. Replacements expand $N, ${N} and $name as regex-automata's interpolation does (the regex crate's rule): the longest name wins, so a group followed by a letter, digit or _ needs braces, ${1}x. $0 is the whole match and $$ a literal $; & and \N are literal. \n, \t and \\ are a newline, a tab and a backslash, as in Evil.

rules.rule: language indentation waits for modes
rules.evil: In emacs-lisp-mode and python-mode, a new line is indented by the language.
rules.die_vim: Until file-type modes (M1) give die-vim a language's indentation, a new line is indented like the line above, as Evil does in text.

rules.rule: the cursor rests on a grapheme's start
rules.evil: e and $ onto a letter with a combining mark leave the cursor after the mark, on the space or the newline: Emacs's command loop pushes point out of a composition. It isn't Evil's grammar.
rules.die_vim: As in Vim: e and $ land on the letter the mark sits on, so e on café lands on the é, mid-line and at a line's end. Another e moves on from there, as Evil's does. An inclusive operator takes the whole grapheme. So do x, X, s, r, ~ and an operator over h or l, where Evil's take a character and split a letter from its mark. h and l on their own step over a grapheme in both.

rules.rule: an operator takes only a motion or a text object
rules.evil: Any other command after an operator runs as if it were a motion: dA deletes to the end of the line, and dI back to the indentation. Some commands (x, y, p, Esc) quit instead.
rules.die_vim: Every key that isn't a motion, a text object or the operator's own key cancels it, quietly, as contract §7 says, so the key doesn't go on to do anything. As in Vim, except that Vim beeps.

rules.rule: a string that never closes isn't a string
rules.evil: When the quotes in the text don't pair up and the cursor is in or before the last one, di" deletes from the quote, or sometimes the character before it, to the end of the text less its last character, or fails, depending on what's earlier in the text.
rules.die_vim: As in Vim: it fails with No quoted string found. Inside a " string that never closes, i' and i` still look in that string, as Evil's do.

rules.rule: a named register lasts for one command
rules.evil: A "x before an h, l or f that fails stays named for the next command, because those motions reset this-command when they signal.
rules.die_vim: As in Vim: the failed command uses it up.

rules.rule: R's backspace takes back a newline
rules.evil: In replace state, <BS> over a newline typed there deletes it and inserts the character after it a second time: Rx<CR><BS><BS> on abc gives abbc.
rules.die_vim: As in Vim: <BS> puts back what the key took, and a newline took nothing, so abc stays abc.

rules.rule: u after a macro undoes more
rules.evil: Emacs's undo counts an undo as an edit unless the last command was also an undo, so a macro's u then a typed u gets the first one back: xx, @a holding u, then u on abcd gives cd.
rules.die_vim: Each u goes back one step, whatever typed or fed it: abcd.

rules.rule: a block insert in a macro goes in on every line
rules.evil: What's typed in a block's I reaches the other lines by a command hook, and macros run without hooks: replaying qa<C-v>jIX<Esc>q gives XXab and Xcd.
rules.die_vim: As in Vim: it goes in on every line, however it was typed.

rules.rule: gv after undoing what took its text
rules.evil: Emacs's undo moves markers back with the text: vjdu then gv ends on the old head.
rules.die_vim: die-core's undo doesn't move markers back, so gv's ends stay where the delete put them: at its start.

rules.rule: brackets around one character
rules.evil: A second i( on a selection of one character, itself inside brackets: on ((a)) it fails with (1, 2) selected, and on ((a) b) from the inner opening bracket it selects (1, 6).
rules.die_vim: A selection of one character counts as none, as Evil's word objects do, so the second i( finds what the first did.

rules.rule: a failed search is an error
rules.evil: isearch only says it failed: /zzz<CR> on text without zzz signals nothing, and the next key runs.
rules.die_vim: As Vim's: it's an error, so what follows it in a macro is dropped (contract §7). Typed keys still run, so the result is your Evil's, with the error added.

rules.rule: a failed search in a macro
rules.evil: The oracle's batch Emacs dies when isearch fails inside a keyboard macro, so there's no fixture of what your Evil does.
rules.die_vim: The macro stops at the search: the keys after it don't run.

rules.rule: the change list
rules.evil: `g;`, `g,` and the mark `.` call goto-chg, which your Emacs doesn't have, so each signals that goto-last-change is void and nothing moves.
rules.die_vim: Vim's: a list per buffer of where changes were, where a change on the same line and fewer than 79 columns from the last replaces it. `.` is the newest. A count that goes too far stops at the list's end, and going on from that end is an error.

cases.note: `.` is the last line :s changed, as in Vim

rules.rule: no sentence motions, so no marks ( and )
rules.evil: `( and `) run evil-backward-sentence-begin and evil-forward-sentence-begin, and ( and ) are those motions.
rules.die_vim: Scope section 10 has no sentence motions, so ( and ) aren't bound, and `( and `) say the marker isn't set. m( and m) are errors in both.

rules.rule: a count of zero
rules.evil: C-u 0 is Emacs's prefix argument of 0, so j moves nothing. Only C-u can type it, since a bare 0 is a motion.
rules.die_vim: A count of 0 counts as no count, as for every other motion here, so j moves one line.

rules.rule: an operator C-u cuts short
rules.evil: d then C-u deletes an empty range: every kill register and the clipboard end up holding empty text, and what they held is gone. C-u's count then goes to the next command.
rules.die_vim: The same, except that the operator kills nothing, so the registers and the clipboard stay as they were.
